The chapters before this one ask how far a vector with a distance can carry each property of meaning, and they say where it stops. This epilogue keeps the ideas about meaning that no current technology satisfies: each section states an idea, the tradition that reached it first, and what the technologies of the book lack for it. Nothing here is a result. The sections are short on purpose, and each is a candidate for a chapter, for `notes/ideas.qmd`, or for deletion.

## Meaning Is Not One Thing {#sec-meaning-meaning}
Ogden and Richards listed sixteen senses of "meaning" and drew the triangle of symbol, thought and referent [@ogden1923meaning]. A vector models the edge between the symbol and the thought, which is Frege's sense, and the edge from the thought to the referent is what grounding would add [@frege1892sense]. Peirce's version is not made of pairs: a sign stands for an object to an interpretant, the three-way relation cannot be resolved into pairs, and the interpretant is itself a sign [@peirce1931collected]. A table of embeddings is dyadic, token to token; what a downstream use supplies to a vector (a retrieval step, a generation step) may be the interpretant, and his pragmatic maxim would test an embedding by what it lets one do (speculation). What current technologies lack: a third term, and a statement of which sense of "meaning" a given space carries.

## The Perfect Language {#sec-perfect-language}
The dream of a sign that reveals the thing [@eco1995search]: the Adamic language, Llull's wheels, and Wilkins's *Real Character* [@wilkins1668essay], a hand-built taxonomy in which the spelling of a word is its address. Borges's critique is that every taxonomy is arbitrary [@borges1964other], and Locke had diagnosed the abuse of words [@locke1694essay]. Eco's dictionary (a tree) against the encyclopedia (a network without a root) is the choice between hierarchy and graph, and the reply from cognitive science is that the form can be learned too (a tree for living kinds, rings, chains and grids elsewhere). What current technologies lack: a way to learn the form of the structure and not only the positions inside a fixed form.

## Methods of Harris That Nobody Uses {#sec-harris-unused}
Harris's paper holds readings that no chapter has taken [@harris1954distributional]. He tests whether a rare construction occurs by asking an informant to complete frames (pp. 161–162), a method of eliciting and not of waiting for the corpus; the modern counterpart would generate targeted probes for the rare cases of a space. He places tentative morpheme boundaries where the number of different continuations rises (§2.2, p. 155), a criterion that could be compared with the frequency merges of byte-pair encoding. He orders the statements from the most inclusive to the subsidiary corrections so that the list can be stopped at any point (p. 147), which is the shape of nested embeddings. And converses such as buy and sell have regular, partly inverted selections, while a discourse has its own substitution sets (p. 160). What current technologies lack: elicitation as a method, and discourse-local sets as an explicit object.

## Meaning for a Body That Acts {#sec-life-makes-meaning}
In biology meaning is functional, what a signal does for a living system, which is Weaver's level C and not B [@weaver1949recent; @maynardsmith2000concept]. Skyrms's signalling games show conventions and their information content emerging from repeated interaction [@skyrms2010signals]; Uexküll's Umwelt says that the dog lives in a space of meanings of its own [@uexkull2010foray]; D'Arcy Thompson's transformations between related forms are diffeomorphisms [@thompson1917growth]; and autopoiesis treats the organism as a maker of meaning [@maturana1980autopoiesis]. What current technologies lack: a space that two agents build between them by acting, and the reversal of the dog test (what is the dog's embedding of us?).

## Part and Whole, Round and Round {#sec-literature-laboratory-meaning}
Writers ran the thought experiments first. Swift's engine writes books by random combination of words, and its sages carry the things themselves [@swift1726gulliver]; Borges's Library of Babel is the space of all strings, almost all of it meaningless, and Funes remembers everything and therefore cannot think, compression being the condition of generalization [@borges1962labyrinths]. Metaphor as a mapping between domains [@lakoff1980metaphors] is the literary form of transport between spaces, and the hermeneutic circle, in which the whole is read through its parts and the parts through the whole [@gadamer1960wahrheit], may be the right reading of contextual vectors. What current technologies lack: a representation of a text in which the part and the whole constrain each other, and not only a part that reads its surroundings.

## Relations Fix the Object {#sec-mathematics-meaning}
The relational thesis has an exact form. The Yoneda lemma says that an object is determined up to isomorphism by its relations to all the others, Firth's slogan as a theorem [@maclane1971categories; @bradley2022enriched]; compositional distributional semantics is a functor from grammar to vector spaces [@coecke2010mathematical]; Klein's Erlangen programme says that a geometry is what its symmetries leave invariant [@klein1893comparative]; and a chord is a point of a quotient space whose orbifold is not Euclidean [@tymoczko2006geometry]. What current technologies lack: a semantics built on these forms and tested against a trained space, and the quotient by the nuisance symmetries of a perceiver.

## A Cost or an Impossibility {#sec-ignoramus-et-ignorabimus}
In 1872 du Bois-Reymond argued that natural science has limits it can never cross, "ignoramus et ignorabimus" [@duboisreymond1872grenzen]; Hilbert answered "we must know, we will know" [@hilbert1930naturerkennen]; Kant had drawn the boundary earlier [@kant1781critique]. The position of the book, that a limit of a vector is a cost and not an impossibility, is a position in that argument, and the question is which limits are costs, which are limits of finite data and which, if any, are neither. What current technologies lack: a way to tell a cost from an impossibility other than waiting.

## What Finite Data Cannot Fix {#sec-what-finite-data-cannot}
Many geometries fit the same finite corpus, so meaning from use alone is underdetermined. Hume found no non-circular justification for inference from the observed to the unobserved [@hume1748enquiry]; Goodman's grue shows that finite data do not fix which predicates project [@goodman1955fact]; Kripke's Wittgenstein asks whether I mean plus or quus [@kripke1982wittgenstein]; and learning theory states it as theorems, a learner without a bias can only memorize and averaged over all targets no algorithm beats another. "Company" is the inductive bias of the book. What current technologies lack: a statement of what they assume about the world (the manifold hypothesis is one) that can be tested, and not only used.

## Does Structure Fix Meaning? {#sec-does-structure-fix-meaning}
A purely relational space cannot tell apart two meanings with the same relations, and two trained spaces differ by an isometry. Newman objected to Russell that if only the structure of the world is known the claim reduces to a statement about how many things there are [@newman1928russell]; Putnam's model-theoretic argument says that use does not fix reference, since any theory constrained by use has unintended models [@putnam1981reason]; Davidson argued that total untranslatability between schemes is incoherent [@davidson1974very]. The answer may be an anchor outside the space (Lewis's eligibility read as the name of what grounding does, speculation). What current technologies lack: an account of what, besides the pattern, fixes meaning, and a test of it.

## What a System Cannot Say About Itself {#sec-what-system-cannot-say}
No space contains a verified account of its own outputs. Rice's theorem has its roots in Gödel's incompleteness [@godel1931formal] and Tarski's result that the truth of a rich language cannot be defined inside it [@tarski1944semantic]; Priest argued that the paradoxes of totality share one structure and that some contradictions are true [@priest2002beyond], and Franzén lists what Gödel's theorems do not imply [@franzen2005godel]. A graded similarity is the book's answer to Rice, and the same pattern predicts that "the set of all meanings" cannot be a point of any one space (speculation). The formal counterpart of "false against unknown" is refutable against independent: a statement that is neither provable nor refutable is ignorance in principle. What current technologies lack: a representation that keeps refuted and independent apart.

## Compression and the Number of Dimensions {#sec-compression-capacity-learnability}
How many dimensions does meaning need, and what does a fixed dimension lose? Kolmogorov defined the information in an object as the length of its shortest program [@kolmogorov1965three]; the information bottleneck keeps only what is relevant to a target [@tishby1999information]; and Minsky and Papert's result on the single-layer perceptron, repaired by a hidden layer, is the template of a limit paid for with more structure [@minsky1969perceptrons]. Choosing the dimension is a code-length trade-off. What current technologies lack: a principled choice of dimension, and a measure of what is lost that is not itself incomputable.

## Deciding Without Knowing the Possibilities {#sec-deciding-without-knowing-possibilities}
The probabilities of a model sum to one over a list fixed by its training, and the world may hold events outside the list. Knight separated measurable risk from unmeasurable uncertainty [@knight1921risk]; Good's missing mass asks how much probability the unseen deserves [@good1953population]; Taleb argues what goes wrong when thin-tailed statistics meet fat tails [@taleb2020statistical]. Under a closed-world default what is not derivable is false, and under an open-world one it is unknown; a softmax over a fixed vocabulary is a closed list, and a nearest-neighbour query always returns $k$ neighbours even when nothing relevant exists. Human decision making is the other half: the Allais and Ellsberg choices and the conjunction fallacy break the rules of probability, and quantum-inspired models of them were studied in the earlier plan and left out of the chapters because no test beat a real-valued baseline (the sections are kept in `embedding-technologies-stubs/complex_plane_quantum_logic.qmd`). What current technologies lack: an open world, and a model of how people decide without one.

## How Reasoners Go Wrong {#sec-how-reasoners-go-wrong}
A chain of thought can be plausible without being what produced the answer, and a reward is a proxy. Bacon's Idols of the Marketplace are the errors that come from words [@bacon1620novum]; Tversky and Kahneman's programme is the modern catalogue [@tversky1974judgment], and people report their mental processes by applying plausible theories and not by introspection [@nisbett1977telling], the human precedent of an unfaithful explanation. For a model, bias is a property of the corpus (what was written, by whom, selected how) and fallacy a property of use. What current technologies lack: an explanation that is faithful to the computation behind it.

## Language, Thought and Translation {#sec-language-thought-translation}
Whorf held that the structure of a language shapes habitual thought [@whorf1956language]; Benjamin held that a translation points toward a shared target that no single language contains [@benjamin1923aufgabe]; Steiner that all understanding is translation [@steiner1975after]. The universal translator is the extreme case: can the calls of a bird, the clicks of a dolphin or the codas of a sperm whale be placed in the same space as a human language, with no translated sentence to learn from? A fourth case varies the artifact: a mechanism with no documentation, such as a piece of extraterrestrial technology or part of a brain, where the question is what it would mean to understand a circuit; Ashby asked it of a sealed box (notes/function_of_physical_systems.md). What current technologies lack: a space built from what a mechanism does, and a translation with no parallel data and no check.

## Limits That May Not Be Costs {#sec-limits-that-may-be}
What it is like to be a bat is not captured by any third-person description [@nagel1974bat]; Mary's room and cognitive closure make related points, and Chalmers named the hard problem of why there is experience [@chalmers1995facing]. Polanyi's "we know more than we can tell" [@polanyi1966tacit] and Dreyfus's background of embodied know-how are the tacit side. The book models what can be said in terms of relations and does not claim to cross these boundaries; the dog test does not address experience. What current technologies lack: nothing that is known to be missing, which is the point.

## Chomsky Against Statistics {#sec-chomsky-against-statistics}
Chomsky's review of Skinner argued that language needs internal representations, which is what probing finds inside language models; "colorless green ideas sleep furiously" said that grammaticality is not probability [@chomsky1957syntactic], and Pereira answered with a class-based bigram model [@pereira2000formal]; Norvig answered the dismissal of statistical models [@norvig2011chomsky]. The debate is not settled by performance because each side measures something else, E-language for the models and I-language for Chomsky; children learn from fewer than 100 million words [@warstadt2023findings], and hierarchical generalization is something sequential networks miss and transformers learn late. What current technologies lack: data efficiency, and a test of I-language.

## The Other Meaning of Meaning {#sec-final-geek-musings-where}
The meaning of a life (Frankl [@frankl1962man]) and meaning as something people do together (Bruner [@bruner1990acts]) are Weaver's level C and lie outside any embedding. The apophatic tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius [@pseudodionysius1987complete] says what can be said only by saying what it is not, the limit of a geometry that knows things by their neighbours; the last proposition of the *Tractatus* [@wittgenstein1922tractatus] says what we cannot speak of we must pass over in silence. What current technologies lack: the question itself. Where does human intuition live in a latent space?

## Promises to Keep {#sec-promises-keep}

*Shelf life.* The sceptics are read with a grain of salt as well. Queen and Zou retested 50 widely cited findings about large language models on 20 newer models and report, in the secondary accounts that this book has read so far, that most no longer held or had weakened within about 15 months [@queen2026shelflife]; the study is about language-model behaviour, and carrying it over to embedding properties is an extrapolation of this book, to be tested, not a result. It cuts both ways. A negative finding made on one family of models (analogies in static word vectors, 2016 to 2019) may not carry over to the models of today, and a positive one may not either: the convergence claim of 2024 [@huh2024platonic] was already qualified in 2026 [@groger2026aristotelian; @koepke2026plato]. Each chapter therefore labels each claim by its kind and its date: a derivation (the offset method as a combination of three similarities [@levy2014linguistic]) lasts as long as its assumptions; a measurement on a model family (the failure of the vanilla offset [@linzen2016analogies]) is a record of that family at that date; a benchmark verdict depends on the benchmark and the model version. When a script of a chapter reruns on a newer model, the change in its numbers is itself a measurement of the shelf life of the property.

*Plan (half a page).* Balance: for each property the chapter that carries it gives what supports it, what the sceptics showed, and what survives; the properties do not stand equally. Nearness and difference are the best documented and the most qualified; direction holds for some qualities and fails for others; region, paths and the senses are weakly tested, and composition must be built. Findings: the properties that the chapters test, each stated in the plain language of distance and direction, and each in the chapter that earns it (the `@sec-prop-*` sections). Achieved: to be collected here from the answer boxes of the chapters, since each property is an expectation that a chapter has to deliver, test or refute. Computation: no property says how a space is computed; whether the way a space is built (memory, cost per step, parallelism) decides which properties it can have is a question for the chapters ahead. Still out of reach: the list is open by design and is not a claim that these are all; a property earns its place by being tested by a chapter and sourced by someone other than the author.

## Scorecard {#sec-tests-scorecard}

One row per chapter and test, filled as chapters are written. *Literature* is the result of the same approach in the literature, *Ours* the smoke test of the chapter, and *Date, model* the date and the model family of the evidence. The table has no total, because a profile across tests and rungs is not an average (a chapter can reach one test and have nothing to say on the others).

| Chapter | Test | Rung | Probe | Literature | Ours | Verdict | Date, model |
|:------------|:---------|:--------|:------------|:--------------|:-----------|:----------|:--------------|
| (none yet) | | | | | | | |

Rules for adding a row.

- The benchmark follows the question of the chapter, and the table may say "no honest probe" for a chapter.
- The number that matters is the literature number for the same approach; ours is a smoke test, run on a laptop, which can fail and cannot rank methods at scale.
- Fix the probe and the literature row before writing the chapter, and record failures. A chapter written to hit a rung stops testing anything.
- Sceptics are part of the row, with their sources (each chapter collects the sceptics of its own question).
